chunk_findings.detail: The new bucketing treats only `state == "running"` as "keep in full", so every job whose status is `"elsewhere"` (unended job started on another host — the state that carries the tail text "check it on that host") is pushed into `others` and therefore collapsed or dropped. That contradicts both the change's own docstring ("exited or killed jobs of OTHER items" collapse) and the README addition ("Running jobs … are listed in full"): an `elsewhere` job is *not* exited or killed, it is alive/unverifiable on another host, which is exactly the case the existing tail text exists to warn about ("WAIT for it; do not start it again" / "check it on that host"). Concrete input: `state.jobs` holds 7 unended jobs — one belonging to `B-mine`, six belonging to other items that were launched on host H2, so `J.status(j).state == "elsewhere"` for those six (this brief runs on H1). Running `ddflow brief --item B-mine` gives `keep = 0`, so all six go into `others`, `hidden = 6`, and the output is the item's own job plus the line "- _6 more unended job(s) (other items', not running): `ddflow job list` shows them…_". The alive-on-H2 jobs — and the "check it on that host"/do-not-restart warning the original code printed for each — vanish entirely, even though under the stated rule ("the item's own jobs and **running** ones in full") they should have been listed. The same misclassification bites a plain `brief`: with more than `BRIEF_OTHER_JOBS` `elsewhere` jobs, the oldest of these alive-but-unverified jobs are silently folded into the "(older, not running)" count line.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py::_brief_jobs (the `s.state == "running"` classification)

chunk_findings.detail: The new partition treats only the literal state `"running"` as "must be shown in full"; every other unended state is dropped into `others`. But the status map used two lines below acknowledges a fourth state, `"elsewhere"` (tail text "check it on that host"), which is precisely a job that was started on another host and whose liveness cannot be verified from here — i.e. an unended job that may still be running. Concrete case: a job `B-other` registered on host `buildbox` is still running remotely (state `"elsewhere"`), and the user runs `ddflow brief --item B-af-signals`. With `item` set, `keep == 0`, so `B-other` is classified as an "other" and never enters `shown`; the brief emits only the count line `_N more unended job(s) (other items', not running): ddflow job list shows them...`. The job's `ELSEWHERE ... check it on that host` line and its warning are gone, and the count line asserts it is "not running" when in fact liveness is unknown/possibly live — exactly the case the docstring says is "the most expensive thing to restart by accident". Before the change every unended job was printed, so this is a new information loss for remote jobs, not just a collapse of exited/gone ones.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/views/markdown.py — `_brief_jobs` classification `s.state == "running"`

chunk_findings.detail: `_project` creates all 40 “other” jobs with `"pid": 0` and states in the comment that this means “never running”. That premise is unsafe: `pid 0` is not a sentinel for a dead process. A standard liveness check such as `os.kill(pid, 0)` succeeds for pid 0, because the call targets the caller’s process group. If the implementation detects running jobs that way, every ONE of the OTHER jobs will be classified as running; the fix’s intended behaviour is to list running jobs in full, so `Jother000` will appear in the brief and the assertion `assert "Jother000" not in text` (and the `f"{STALE} more unended job(s)"` collapse assertion) will fail on correct code. The test should use a pid that reliably raises `ProcessLookupError` (e.g., a large unused pid) or mock the liveness check.

chunk_findings.detail: The change moves every job whose status is `"elsewhere"` into the "shown in full" set unconditionally: `live = s.state in ("running", "elsewhere")` and then `shown if live or (item and j.item == item) else others`. Only the `item`-matching jobs and genuinely-running jobs should be exempt from the collapse; "not checkable here" is not the same as "about the asked-for item", so the rest (including other items' elsewhere jobs) should fall into the count line.

chunk_findings.detail: The guard is on the wrong call. `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` is evaluated *before* the `try`, so only the `before` lookup is protected by `except (ValueError, OSError)`. But `_range_problems` can raise for the *after* text for exactly the same reasons — the fact that the new `except` catches `OSError` proves the failure mode is not "the edited text does not load" (that would be `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`, a `ValueError`), but a filesystem read/merge of the sibling layer inside `_effective(repo, text, local)`. `Config.check` is run on the single edited file, not on the merged effective config, so the docstring's claim "the edited text itself has already passed `Config.check`" does not make `found` safe. Concrete scenario: editing the committed layer with `ddflow config --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6` while the git-ignored `.ddflow/local` layer is unreadable (`chmod 000`) or malformed; the edited text passes `Config.check`, then `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` merges the broken local layer and raises `OSError`/`ValueError`, which now propagates out of `_new_range_problems` uncaught instead of being swallowed. Before this change the entire body of `_range_problems` was wrapped in `except Exception: return set()`, so both the `before` and `after` lookups degraded to an empty set and the command completed (no range refusal). Because the sibling layer is the same for `before` and `after`, the `except` around the `before` call can essentially never help: whenever the sibling layer is the failure cause, `found` raises first and the except is unreachable. The fix is to move `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` inside the `try` (or wrap both lookups), restoring the previous always-tolerant behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail:
The detail string for the explicit-`max_parallel_tasks`/old-4 case still hardcodes the committed-layer command:

    f"{OLD_PARALLEL_DEFAULT}: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`; "

This ignores the layer of `schedule.parallel`. If the user's local layer contains `schedule.parallel = "auto"` (the intent explicitly supports setting these knobs in the git-ignored local layer, e.g. `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6`), then the local value overrides whatever the committed file says. Concretely:

1. Committed `.ddflow/config.toml` (written by an old `adopt`) has `[schedule] max_parallel_tasks = 4` — the finding fires because the effective value is 4 and it is explicit.
2. `.ddflow/local/config.toml` has `schedule.parallel = "auto"` (user opted into adaptive on this machine).
3. The note tells the user: "To keep exactly 4: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`".

The old call site was:

```python
_range_problems(repo, text, local) - _range_problems(repo, text_before, local)
```

where each `_range_problems` wrapped its `_effective` call in `except Exception: return set()`. chunk_findings.detail: The guard is on the wrong call. `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` is evaluated *before* the `try`, so only the `before` lookup is protected by `except (ValueError, OSError)`. But `_range_problems` can raise for the *after* text for exactly the same reasons — the fact that the new `except` catches `OSError` proves the failure mode is not "the edited text does not load" (that would be `tomllib.TOMLDecodeError`, a `ValueError`), but a filesystem read/merge of the sibling layer inside `_effective(repo, text, local)`. `Config.check` is run on the single edited file, not on the merged effective config, so the docstring's claim "the edited text itself has already passed `Config.check`" does not make `found` safe. chunk_findings.detail:
The old call site was:

```python
_range_problems(repo, text, local) - _range_problems(repo, text_before, local)
```

where each `_range_problems` wrapped its `_effective` call in `except Exception: return set()`. The new code computes `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` **outside** any `try`, and catches only `(ValueError, OSError)` around the `before` evaluation. Both the pre-edit and post-edit evaluations have therefore lost the blanket `except Exception`.

Concrete failure: a project whose on-disk config makes `_effective` raise something outside `(ValueError, OSError)` — e.g. the project's `ConfigError` raised for an invalid `[schedule]` value such as `parallel = "bogus"` (the caller catches `ConfigError` separately from `(TOMLDecodeError, ValueError)`, so it is not necessarily a `ValueError`). A user then runs the *repair* edit, `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel auto`, which makes the after-text pass `Config.check`, so execution reaches `_new_range_problems`. `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` succeeds, but the guarded call `_range_problems(repo, before, local)` raises `ConfigError`, which is not in `(ValueError, OSError)`, so it escapes and `ddflow config` aborts with a traceback instead of writing the repair. The docstring explicitly promises the opposite ("When the config before the edit cannot be judged, nothing can be attributed to the edit and nothing is refused"), and the old `except Exception` did allow exactly this repair. The same regression applies to the unguarded `found` line: any pre-edit failure mode of `_effective` that the old code swallowed for the after-text now propagates.

(Not reported: the flowparams fixed-mode mapping and the `min<=start<=max` handling, which look correct given the stated validation, and the README/doc-string requirements, which cannot be judged from this diff.)

Before this change the entire body of `_range_problems` was wrapped in `except Exception: return set()`, so both the `before` and `after` lookups degraded to an empty set and the command completed (no range refusal). Because the sibling layer is the same for `before` and `after`, the `except` around the `before` call can essentially never help: whenever the sibling layer is the failure cause, `found` raises first and the except is unreachable. The fix is to move `found = _range_problems(repo, after, local)` inside the `try` (or wrap both lookups), restoring the previous always-tolerant behaviour.

chunk_findings.detail:
The detail string for the explicit-`max_parallel_tasks`/old-4 case still hardcodes the committed-layer command:

    f"{OLD_PARALLEL_DEFAULT}: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`; "

This ignores the layer of `schedule.parallel`. If the user's local layer contains `schedule.parallel = "auto"` (the intent explicitly supports setting these knobs in the git-ignored local layer, e.g. `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_max 6`), then the local value overrides whatever the committed file says. Concretely:

1. Committed `.ddflow/config.toml` (written by an old `adopt`) has `[schedule] max_parallel_tasks = 4` — the finding fires because the effective value is 4 and it is explicit.
2. `.ddflow/local/config.toml` has `schedule.parallel = "auto"` (user opted into adaptive on this machine).
3. The note tells the user: "To keep exactly 4: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`".
4. Running it writes `parallel = "fixed"` into the committed layer, which is overridden by the local `auto`, so the effective mode stays auto and the promised "keep exactly 4" is not achieved — the suggested command is a silent no-op.

The correct remedy (and the one the rest of the change establishes as the rule) is `_set_cmd(cfg, "schedule.parallel", "fixed")`, yielding `ddflow config --local --set schedule.parallel fixed` in this scenario. The changed tests only cover the layer-aware path for `worktree.max_parallel` (`test_a_local_cap_is_given_a_local_remedy`); no test exercises a local `schedule.parallel`, so this gap passes CI.
chunk_findings.title: ddflow/services/workflow.py:_parallel_findings (the `schedule.max_parallel_tasks` note)

chunk_findings.detail:
The new test asserts that `_new_range_problems(repo, "", "[schedule]
max_parallel_tasks = 10
", True) == set()`, i.e. that the range guard reports *no* problem for a start value of 10 while the sibling layer is a syntactically broken TOML file. But the ceiling that makes 10 invalid is the shipped default `schedule.max_parallel_max = 8`, which does not live in the unreadable layer at all — it is knowable independently of it. The pre-existing test in the same file (`assert _new_range_problems(repo, "", after, False)` with `after = "[schedule]
max_parallel_tasks = 10
"`) already shows that this exact value/`before=""` combination is supposed to be flagged as out of range. So the new test enshrines a behavior where a single TOML syntax error anywhere in the committed layer silently disables the ceiling check for a different key: `ddflow config --local --set schedule.max_parallel_tasks 10` (or `--set schedule.max_parallel_max 3` etc.) is accepted instead of being reported, contradicting the stated requirement that out-of-range schedule knobs produce a config error (exit 3) naming the key. The correct defensive behavior is to swallow the parse failure only as far as avoiding a crash and to keep validating against the package-default floor/ceiling (and to let the normal config-load path surface the broken layer as exit 3); returning `set()` unconditionally on sibling read failure drops the range invariant entirely.
chunk_findings.title: tests/test_adaptive_config.py :: test_an_unreadable_sibling_layer_never_crashes_the_range_guard

chunk_findings.detail:
The remedy command's layer is now chosen from the layer of `schedule.max_parallel_tasks`, but the command *sets* `schedule.parallel`, whose effective layer is decided by `schedule.parallel` itself. When the two keys live in different layers, the printed command no longer does what the message promises.

Concrete failure: committed `.ddflow/config.toml` contains the old adopted default `[schedule] max_parallel_tasks = 4`, and `.ddflow/local/config.toml` contains `[schedule] parallel = "auto"` (a per-machine override, exactly the case the feature advertises: "a local-layer value overrides the committed one"). The finding fires (effective `parallel` is auto and `max_parallel_tasks` is the old default), and the tail of the message offers "To keep exactly 4: `ddflow config --set schedule.parallel fixed`" — because `_in_local(cfg, 'schedule.max_parallel_tasks')` is false, no `--local` is emitted. Running that command writes `parallel = fixed` into the committed layer, which the pre-existing local `parallel = "auto"` still overrides, so the effective value stays `auto` and the limit can still rise above 4. The user cannot reach the state the message describes.

This is a regression from the pre-change behavior: `_set_cmd(cfg, 'schedule.parallel', 'fixed')` checked `_in_local(cfg, 'schedule.parallel')`, which is true here, so it emitted `ddflow config --local --set schedule.parallel fixed` and actually took effect. The new `layer_of` argument also contradicts its own docstring ("a machine's own override must not be answered in the shared file") in this case: the machine's override is on `schedule.parallel`, and the answer is placed in the shared file anyway. The fix should key the layer off the key being set, or off whichever of the two keys is more specific (local wins), rather than unconditionally off `layer_of`.

chunk_findings.detail: The new code conflates two different causes of `judged(after, local) is None`: the *sibling* (committed) layer being unreadable, and the *edit text* `after` itself being unreadable. In the old code the sibling-broken case was handled by `found = _range_problems(repo, after, False)` (which succeeds only because `after` was assumed to parse), and if `after` itself could not be loaded that second call raised `unreadable` out of `_new_range_problems`, so the caller saw the failure. In the new code the retry is wrapped as `judged(after, False) or set()`: for an edit text that does not load, `judged(after, False)` is again `None`, so `found` becomes `set()`, `had` is subtracted from it, and the function returns the empty set — i.e. "this edit introduces no new problems". Demonstration: with a valid committed layer and `before` valid, call `_new_range_problems(repo, before, '[schedule]\nmax_parallel_min = "x"\n', True)`. `judged(after, True)` raises (bad type raises `ValueError`, exactly as the new test relies on for `adapt_up_after_s = "x"`), `local` is flipped to `False`, and the retry over the defaults raises the same way, so the result is `set()`. `_range_refusal(set())` then yields no refusal and the caller is free to write a layer whose merged config cannot load; previously that failure propagated. The added test only exercises an unloadable *before*, so this path is untested, and the docstring's own principle ("a broken sibling never switches the guard off") is violated in the other direction: a broken edit text silently switches the range guard off.
